h1: Personal Injury Lawyer in El Paso, Texas
intro: If you were hurt in a crash in El Paso County because of someone else's carelessness, attorney Robert Navar can review what happened, explain how a Texas injury claim works, and handle the insurance company so you can concentrate on treatment.
summaryHeading: Injured in an El Paso crash? Start with these four things
summary: Get checked by a doctor even if you feel fine at the scene. Some injuries show up days later, and a gap in treatment makes a claim harder to document.
Do not give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurance company before you have talked to a lawyer. You are not required to, and what you say can be used to reduce or deny the claim.

In Texas you generally have two years from the date of the injury to file a lawsuit, with some exceptions. Evidence such as camera footage and witness contact information disappears much faster than that.

sections.heading: What Happens at the First Consultation
paragraphs: The first meeting is a conversation, not a sales pitch. Mr. Navar wants to know how the crash happened, what the police report says, what injuries you have, where you have been treated, and what the insurance companies have said so far. From that he can give you a candid view of whether a claim is worth pursuing. The consultation is free, in English or Spanish, by phone or at the office at 11860 Vista Del Sol Dr. #119 on the East Side.

You will not hear a dollar figure for your case or a promise about the result; no responsible lawyer can value an injury claim before treatment is finished and the records are in hand. What you will hear is an explanation of the damages Texas law recognizes — medical expenses, lost earnings, physical pain, mental anguish and, in cases of gross negligence, exemplary damages — and how each would be proven.

If you decide to hire the office, the fee arrangement is put in writing first. Injury cases are typically handled on a contingency-fee basis, meaning the fee is a share of any recovery rather than an hourly bill; the percentage, case expenses and what happens if there is no recovery are set out in that written agreement.

sections.heading: After You Hire the Office: How a Claim Moves
paragraphs: Once the agreement is signed, the office sends letters of representation to every insurer involved. From then on the adjusters contact the attorney, not you, which ends the pressure to give a statement or accept an early, low offer. The office also sends preservation requests for evidence that can disappear — business camera footage, event-data-recorder downloads and, in trucking cases, the driver's logs and the carrier's maintenance file.

While you finish treatment, the office collects the medical records and bills, documents lost wages with your employer, and watches the limitations period. When your doctors have a clear picture of your condition, a written demand goes to the insurer with the records attached. Many claims resolve by negotiation after that; if the insurer will not make a reasonable offer, the remaining option is a lawsuit in the El Paso County courts, which Mr. Navar will discuss with you before anything is filed. Timing varies with the injury, the treatment and the insurer's position, so no timeline is promised.

sections.heading: Why a Local El Paso Lawyer, and the Two Texas Rules That Shape Every Claim
paragraphs: Out-of-town advertising firms treat an El Paso crash like any other file. A local office knows the intersections, the adjusters who handle El Paso claims, the local court clerks' practices and the medical providers on both sides of town — and your case is not handed off to a case manager you never meet.

Comparative responsibility. Texas uses a modified comparative-fault rule (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code ch. 33). In general, a person who is found more than half responsible for the crash recovers nothing, and a person who is found partly but not mostly responsible has the recovery reduced in proportion to that share of fault. Insurers lean on this rule, which is why an early recorded statement that "I might have been going a little fast" can cost real money.

The limitations period. Texas generally gives two years from the date of injury to file a personal-injury lawsuit (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code §16.003). There are exceptions that can shorten or extend that period — claims against a city, county or state agency require formal notice much sooner, and different rules apply to minors and wrongful-death claims — so have a lawyer calendar the deadline for your specific facts.

If you have them, attach or text photos of the crash report (or its number), both drivers' insurance cards, any citation, and the adjuster's letter. Were you also ticketed at the scene? faqs.q: How much does it cost to hire a personal injury lawyer in El Paso?
faqs.a: The initial consultation is free. Injury cases are typically handled on a contingency-fee basis — the fee is a share of any recovery rather than an hourly charge — and the exact percentage and how case expenses are handled are set out in the written agreement you sign before work begins.

faqs.q: Should I talk to the other driver's insurance company?
faqs.a: Not before you have spoken with a lawyer. You can confirm basic facts such as the date and your contact information, but anything about fault, your injuries or a settlement should go through your attorney.

faqs.q: How long do I have to file an injury claim in Texas?
faqs.a: Generally two years from the date of the injury, but there are exceptions. Claims against a governmental entity require formal written notice within a much shorter window, and other situations can change the deadline. Have a lawyer confirm the date that applies to your case rather than assuming you have two years.

faqs.q: What if I was partly at fault for the crash?
faqs.a: Texas's modified comparative-fault rule allows a claim as long as you are not found more than half responsible; the recovery is reduced by your share of fault. How fault is divided is often the main dispute in a case, which is one reason not to concede anything to an adjuster early on.

faqs.q: The other driver had no insurance. Do I still have a claim?
faqs.a: Possibly. If your own policy includes uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage or personal injury protection, a claim can be made under your policy. Bring your declarations page to the consultation so the office can check what coverage you actually have.

faqs.q: Do you handle injury cases in Spanish?
faqs.a: Yes. Attorney Robert Navar speaks English and Spanish, and consultations and case updates are available in either language.
